lessons.title: The body of a fish
lessons.html:
Outside parts

  • Skin and scales: protect the fish. The skin is covered with slime (mucus), which keeps germs out. Rough handling removes slime and scales and lets disease in. Catfish have no scales, only skin and slime.
  • Fins: help the fish swim, steer and stay upright. The tail fin pushes the fish forward.
  • Gills: under the gill covers on each side of the head. They take oxygen from the water.
  • Eyes: fish have no eyelids. Strong sunlight and sudden light can stress them.
  • Lateral line: a line along each side of the body. It feels movement and vibration in the water. This is why fish react when someone walks heavily next to a tank.

Inside parts

  • Gut: digests food. Waste comes out as dung.
  • Liver: stores energy and cleans the blood.
  • Kidneys: remove water and some waste.
  • Swim bladder: a bag of air that lets the fish float at the depth it wants without effort.
  • Heart: pumps blood to the gills and the body.
  • Gonads: the parts that make eggs (female) or milt (male).

How fish breathe

Water goes in through the mouth and out over the gills. The gills take dissolved oxygen out of the water and put carbon dioxide and ammonia (waste) into it. Healthy gills are bright red. Pale, brown or swollen gills show a problem. If there is not enough oxygen, fish come to the surface and gasp. This is an emergency.

lessons.title: Fish are cold-blooded
lessons.html:
Water temperature controls the fish

Fish are cold-blooded. Their body is the same temperature as the water around them. They cannot warm themselves up or cool down. This means:

  • In warm water, fish eat more, grow faster and need more oxygen.
  • In cold water, fish eat less and grow slowly.
  • Each species has a range of temperatures it likes. Trout like cold water. Tilapia and catfish like warm water.
  • Sudden temperature changes stress fish. When you move fish from one tank to another, the temperatures must be close. Let the bag or container float in the new water for a while so the temperatures become the same.

Warm water holds less oxygen

Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water. On hot summer days, especially late at night and early in the morning, oxygen in ponds can drop very low. Fish may need extra air from aerators.

Feeding and temperature

Because fish eat less when the water is cold, the farm's feeding chart gives less feed at lower temperatures. Feed that is not eaten rots and makes the water dirty. Always check that fish are eating the feed. If feed is left over, tell your supervisor.

Waste

Fish put waste into the water from their gills and their dung. The main waste is ammonia, which is poisonous to fish at high levels. More feed means more waste. That is why water must be cleaned, changed or filtered.

lessons.title: Shellfish, growth and life cycles
lessons.html:
Shellfish bodies

Abalone

  • Has one shell on top and a big muscular foot underneath. The foot sticks to rocks and tank walls.
  • Breathes with gills under the shell.
  • Eats with a rough tongue that scrapes seaweed.
  • Abalone bleed easily, and a cut foot can kill them. Use a flat, blunt spatula to remove them gently from surfaces.

Mussels and oysters

  • Have two shells joined by a hinge. Strong muscles keep the shells closed.
  • They pump water through their gills and catch tiny food particles. This is called filter feeding.
  • Mussels hold onto ropes with thin threads called the byssus (beard).

Growth

Fish grow all their lives if they have enough food and the right conditions. Growth slows when fish are stressed, crowded, sick, cold or underfed. Farms weigh samples of fish regularly to check growth and work out feed.

Life cycle of a farmed fish

  1. Egg: laid by the female and fertilised by the male.
  2. Larva: hatches from the egg. At first it lives on its yolk sac.
  3. Fry: a tiny fish that starts eating small feed.
  4. Fingerling: about the size of a finger.
  5. Grow-out: the fish grows to selling size.
  6. Brood stock: adult fish kept for breeding.

Key points

  • Slime and scales protect fish; handle gently and with wet hands.
  • Gills take oxygen from water; gasping fish need help at once.
  • Fish are cold-blooded; water temperature controls feeding and growth.
  • Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
  • The fish life cycle runs from egg to larva, fry, fingerling, grow-out and brood stock.
